content: The 2007 update to the Guideline for Isolation Precautions: Preventing Transmission of Infectious Agents in Healthcare Settings builds upon and expands the 1996 guideline, addressing significant developments in healthcare delivery and infection control. These updates reflect the need for recommendations applicable across diverse healthcare settings, including hospitals, long-term care facilities, ambulatory care, home care, and specialty care sites. The revised guideline emphasizes the use of common infection control principles adaptable to specific settings. The term nosocomial infections has been replaced with healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) to account for the evolving patterns of healthcare delivery and the challenges in pinpointing the exact location of exposure to infectious agents. This change acknowledges the difficulty in determining whether infections were acquired within a healthcare facility or elsewhere. Advances in medical technology, such as gene therapy, and concerns about bioterrorism have necessitated a broader scope of issues to be addressed in the updated guidelines. The successful implementation of Standard Precautions, first introduced in 1996, has reaffirmed their role as the foundation for preventing the transmission of infectious agents in all healthcare settings. Additionally, the need for Respiratory Hygiene/Cough Etiquette emerged from lessons learned during the SARS outbreaks, where inadequate source control measures contributed to the spread of the SARS coronavirus (SARS-CoV). The guideline reiterates the importance of safe injection practices, particularly in light of outbreaks of hepatitis B and C in ambulatory settings. It also introduces the use of masks during certain spinal injection procedures to mitigate the risk of meningitis caused by respiratory flora. Furthermore, evidence supporting the role of environmental controls in reducing life-threatening fungal infections in severely immunocompromised patients, such as those undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, has led to updates in the components of the Protective Environment (PE). The guideline highlights the influence of administrative factors, such as nurse staffing levels, safety culture, and organizational support, on adherence to infection control practices. These factors are critical in preventing the transmission of infectious agents. The increasing incidence of HAIs caused by multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) has prompted the inclusion of specific recommendations for surveillance and control measures tailored to various healthcare settings. The document is intended for use by infection control staff, healthcare epidemiologists, administrators, nurses, and other healthcare providers responsible for developing, implementing, and evaluating infection control programs. It also serves as a resource for those involved in public reporting of HAI rates and designing state programs. The guideline reviews scientific data on the transmission of infectious agents in healthcare settings, including discussions on bioaerosols, droplet, and airborne transmission. These topics gained prominence during the 2003 SARS outbreaks, where aerosol-generating procedures were linked to transmission. The guideline also addresses infection risks associated with specific healthcare settings and patient populations. Hand hygiene, barrier precautions, safe work practices, and isolation practices are updated, with new information on healthcare system components influencing transmission risks. The guideline emphasizes the need for adequate infection control staffing and the role of clinical microbiology laboratories in supporting infection control efforts. For the first time, the guideline includes surveillance of healthcare-associated infections, providing valuable information for new infection control professionals and those involved in public reporting programs. It describes the categories of precautions developed by the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), offering guidance for their application in various healthcare settings. The guideline maintains the categories of Transmission-Based Precautions—Contact, Droplet, and Airborne—while introducing a recommendation to don personal protective equipment (PPE) upon entering the room of patients on Contact or Droplet Precautions. This change reflects the unpredictability of patient interactions and the role of contaminated environmental surfaces in pathogen transmission. The Protective Environment (PE) for allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplant patients has been updated, incorporating engineering and design interventions to reduce exposure to environmental fungi during high-risk periods. These measures apply only to acute care hospitals providing care to these patients. The guideline includes tables summarizing key information, such as the evolution of the document, guidance on empiric isolation precautions, infection control recommendations for bioterrorism agents, components of Standard Precautions, and a glossary of definitions. A new addition is a recommended sequence for donning and removing PPE to optimize safety and prevent self-contamination. Appendix A provides an updated alphabetical list of infectious agents and clinical conditions requiring isolation precautions, detailing the type and duration of precautions and adjunctive measures to prevent transmission. Relevant citations are included. The guideline also features a comprehensive review and detailed recommendations for preventing MDRO transmission, published electronically in 2006. It outlines the rationale and institutional requirements for effective MDRO control programs, emphasizing the need for healthcare facilities to prioritize MDRO prevention, implement control measures, and assess program effectiveness. The updated guideline responds to changes in healthcare delivery and addresses new concerns about the transmission of infectious agents to patients and healthcare workers. Its primary objective is to enhance the safety of the healthcare delivery system by reducing HAI rates. It provides evidence-based recommendations for infection control practices across all components of the healthcare system, reaffirming the importance of Standard and Transmission-Based Precautions.
